m1-l1:
Scratch is a free tool made at MIT where you build games, stories, and animations by snapping blocks together, like LEGO bricks that tell a computer what to do. Millions of kids use it. You don't have to type anything, and you can't "break" it. Before our first class, let's get it ready.

What you need

  • A computer. A laptop or desktop with Windows, macOS, or ChromeOS works best. A tablet can work, but dragging blocks with your finger is slower.
  • A web browser. Chrome, Edge, Firefox, or Safari. Keep it up to date.
  • Internet for our live class and for the online editor.
  • A mouse (nice to have). Dragging blocks is much easier with a mouse than with a trackpad.
  • Headphones (nice to have). Scratch projects make sounds, and so will everyone else's at home.

That's it. Scratch is free, and you never have to pay for anything in this class.

Three ways to open Scratch

Pick one. All three give you the same Scratch 3 editor with the same blocks.

Option A: The online editor, no account

This is the fastest way to start.

  1. Open your browser.
  2. Go to scratch.mit.edu/projects/editor.
  3. The editor opens with an orange cat in the middle of a white rectangle. You're in!

You can build anything without an account. The only catch: Scratch won't remember your project for you. You must save it to your computer yourself (we'll practice that in this module).

Option B: The online editor, with an account

A free Scratch account saves your projects online, so you can open them from any computer. It also lets you share projects later in the course.

Watch out

Ask a parent or guardian first. Making an account means giving Scratch an email address. If you're a kid, that should be a grown-up's email, and a grown-up needs to confirm it. Do this together.

  1. Go to scratch.mit.edu and click Join Scratch at the top.
  2. Make a username. Don't use your real name, your school, or your age in it. "PixelTiger42" is great. "EmmaSmith2015" is not.
  3. Make a password you can remember, and keep it secret (except from your grown-up).
  4. Fill in the rest with your grown-up, including the email address.
  5. Your grown-up opens the email from Scratch and clicks the link to confirm the account.
  6. Back on the site, click Create at the top to open the editor.

When you're signed in, your username appears in the top-right corner of the editor.

Option C: The Scratch app (works offline)

If your internet is slow or you want Scratch without a browser, use the app.

  1. Go to scratch.mit.edu/download.
  2. Pick your computer type (Windows, macOS, ChromeOS, or Android) and follow the steps on that page.
  3. Open Scratch from your apps.

The app works without internet, but it doesn't connect to a Scratch account. You'll save projects as files on your computer.

Tip

Not sure which to pick? Start with Option A today. You can always make an account later with your grown-up, and your saved files will still open.

Quick test: does it work?

Let's make sure blocks run on your computer. This tiny script is three blocks long.

  1. On the left side, click the yellow Events circle.
  2. Drag when green flag clicked into the big empty middle area.
  3. Click the purple Looks circle.
  4. Drag say [Hello!] for (2) seconds and snap it under the first block. You'll feel it "click" into place.
  5. Click the pink Sound circle and snap play sound (Meow v) until done under that.

Your script should look like this:

Now click the green flag above the stage (the white area on the right). Here's what happens:

If you saw the bubble and heard the meow, you're ready for class.

If something doesn't work

  • Nothing happens when I click the flag. Check that the blocks are snapped together. If there's a gap between them, drag the lower block up until it clicks.
  • I see the bubble but hear no meow. Check your computer's volume and make sure the browser tab isn't muted.
  • The page is blank or very slow. Try a different browser, or close other tabs. Very old browsers like Internet Explorer can't run Scratch 3.
  • The page asks me to sign in. You don't have to. Go straight to scratch.mit.edu/projects/editor instead of the home page.

Stay safe online

Scratch is a friendly place, and it has rules to keep it that way. Never share your full name, address, school, phone number, or passwords in a project or comment. If anything online makes you uncomfortable, tell a grown-up or your teacher.

Further reading

  • Scratch for parents (opens in a new tab): what Scratch is and how accounts work, written for grown-ups.
  • Scratch Account on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): what an account lets you do.
m1-l2:
Think of the Scratch editor as a kitchen. The blocks are your ingredients, the middle area is your counter where you mix them, and the stage is the plate where everyone sees what you made. Once you know where everything lives, cooking up projects gets fast.

The five parts of the editor

Open the editor (scratch.mit.edu/projects/editor, or the Scratch app). You'll see these parts.

1. The block palette (left)

A column of colored circles, one per category: Motion (blue), Looks (purple), Sound (pink), Events (yellow), Control (gold), Sensing (light blue), Operators (green), Variables (orange), and My Blocks (red). Click a circle and the list jumps to those blocks. Colors help you find blocks again later: if a block is purple, it lives in Looks.

2. The code area (middle)

The big empty space. Drag blocks here and snap them together into scripts. A script is a stack of blocks that runs from top to bottom.

3. The stage (top right)

Where your project plays. Above it are the green flag (start) and the red stop sign (stop everything). The small buttons on the far right change the stage size or go full screen.

4. The sprite pane (bottom right)

Every character or object in your project is a sprite. The cat is a sprite called Sprite1. This pane shows all your sprites and lets you change a sprite's name, position (x and y), size, and direction. The cat-face button in the corner adds a new sprite.

5. The Stage pane and the tabs

Next to the sprite pane is the Stage button, where you pick a backdrop (the background picture). At the top left are three tabs: Code, Costumes, and Sounds. They always show the code, looks, or sounds of whatever sprite is selected.

Tip

Code belongs to the sprite that's highlighted in the sprite pane. If your blocks "vanished," you probably clicked a different sprite. Click the cat again and they'll be back.

Build "Meet Me"

Your first project: the cat walks out, introduces you, and does a little spin. Pick the starter block first.

Step 1: Start with a hat block

Every script needs a "hat" block on top. It has a rounded top and tells Scratch when to run. From Events, drag out when green flag clicked.

Step 2: Put the cat in its starting spot

From Motion, snap go to x: () y: () under the hat. Click each white bubble and type the numbers. We'll learn what x and y mean in Week 1. For now, -150 moves the cat to the left side.

Click the green flag. The cat jumps to the left side of the stage.

Step 3: Walk and talk

Add a glide from Motion and two speech bubbles from Looks. Change the words to be about you.

Click the green flag:

Step 4: Finish with a spin and a meow

The turn right (15) degrees block shows a curved arrow in Scratch. Snap it in twice, plus a sound.

Now the cat flips upside down, flips back, and meows at the end. Each turn of 180 degrees is half a circle, so two of them make one full spin.

Step 5: Pick a backdrop

Click the Choose a Backdrop button (bottom right, under the Stage button). Pick any picture you like. Then click the cat in the sprite pane so your code shows again.

Step 6: Name your project

If you're signed in to a Scratch account, click the title box at the top of the editor (it says Untitled) and type Meet Me. Without an account, you'll name the project when you save it as a file.

Proof it works

Click the green flag and check every box:

  • The cat starts on the left every single time.
  • It glides to the middle.
  • Both speech bubbles show your words.
  • It spins and meows.
  • There's a backdrop behind it.

If all five happen, your Scratch setup works. Save it now: click File > Save to your computer (or File > Save now if you have an account). The next lesson covers saving in detail.

What usually goes wrong

  • The glide doesn't happen. You may have grabbed glide (1) secs to (random position v) instead of the one with x and y. Both are in Motion. Swap it.
  • The cat stays upside down. You only have one turn right (180) degrees block. Add the second one.
  • The cat runs off somewhere weird. Check for a minus sign: -150 and 150 are opposite sides.
  • A block won't snap. Drag it by its left edge and drop it so the top lines up just under the block above. A gray shadow shows where it will land.
  • I clicked a block in the palette and the cat moved. That's fine! Clicking any block runs it once. It's a great way to test.

Further reading

  • Scratch Editor on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): a labeled guide to every part of the screen.
  • Getting Started tutorial (opens in a new tab): the official step-by-step tutorial that opens right inside the editor.
m1-l3:
Imagine spending a whole class building a game, then closing the tab and losing it. It happens to almost everyone once. This lesson makes sure it never happens to you, and shows what our weekly class looks like so you know what to expect.

How our class works

We meet live online once a week for 1.5 hours, for 6 weeks. Each week has three parts, and you'll find all three in this course:

  1. Notes. Your teacher explains the week's new blocks with small examples. Read the Notes lesson again later if something didn't stick.
  2. Code-along. We build one small project together, step by step. Follow along in your own editor. If you fall behind, say so in the chat. That's normal and teachers expect it.
  3. Practice. Short challenges to try on your own, from easy to tricky. Every challenge has a solution, but try first! Peeking too early is like reading the end of a mystery book.

Before each class

  • Open the Scratch editor and test the green flag.
  • Have last week's project file (or your account) ready.
  • Put on headphones if you have them, so project sounds don't get mixed up with the call.

During class

  • Keep the class call in one window and Scratch in another. If you only have one screen, switch between them.
  • Ask questions any time. "My cat disappeared" is a perfectly good question.

Saving without an account

Without an account, Scratch does not save anything for you. You save your project as a file that ends in .sb3.

  1. Click File at the top left.
  2. Click Save to your computer.
  3. Depending on your browser, the file goes straight into your Downloads folder, or a box pops up asking where to save it. If it asks, pick a good folder and type a name.

The file is usually called Scratch Project.sb3 at first. Rename it in your computer's files to something you'll recognize, like week1-meet-me.sb3. Keep the .sb3 at the end.

Watch out

Save again every time you make big changes, and always at the end of class. Saving makes a new copy of the file each time, so use clear names like week2-dance.sb3 and delete old copies you don't need.

Opening your file again

  1. Open the editor.
  2. Click File > Load from your computer.
  3. Find your .sb3 file and open it.

Scratch will ask if you want to replace what's on screen. Say yes only if you've already saved what you were working on.

Saving with an account

If you're signed in, Scratch saves your project online.

  • Scratch saves on its own every few minutes. Click File > Save now whenever you want to be sure.
  • Give each project a name in the title box at the top, so you can find it.
  • File > Save as a copy makes a second version, so you can try a wild idea without wrecking the original.

Finding your projects again

Click the folder icon in the top bar (it's called My Stuff). Every project you've made is listed there, newest first. Click See inside to open one in the editor.

Your projects stay private until you choose to share them. We'll talk about sharing safely at the end of the course.

Organize your work

Make one folder on your computer called Scratch Class. Put every project there, named by week:

Even with an account, downloading a copy at the end of each class is a smart backup.

Fixing common problems

"I clicked the green flag and nothing happened."

Your blocks need a hat block on top, and every block must be snapped in. A loose block sitting a little below the stack won't run. Drag it up until it clicks.

"My sprite disappeared!"

It probably walked off the stage or got hidden. Give every project a reset script like this one, and click the green flag:

What happens:

"I deleted my sprite by mistake."

Click Edit > Restore Sprite right away. It brings back the last sprite you deleted, code and all.

"I deleted some blocks by mistake."

Right-click an empty part of the code area and choose Undo. You can also press Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on a Mac) while the code area is selected.

"My code is a messy pile."

Right-click an empty spot in the code area and choose Clean up Blocks. Scratch lines up all your scripts neatly.

"There's no sound."

Check your computer's volume, make sure the browser tab isn't muted, and check that your headphones are plugged in all the way.

"Load from your computer doesn't show my file."

Look in your Downloads folder. If the file ends in .sb3, it's a Scratch project. If it got renamed to something like .sb3.txt, rename it back to .sb3.

"Scratch is really slow."

Close other tabs and programs. If it's still slow, try a different browser or the Scratch app.

Your setup checklist

Before Week 1, make sure you can do all of these:

  • Open the editor.
  • Run a script with the green flag.
  • Save a project (to your computer or with Save now).
  • Close the editor, open it again, and get your project back.

If you can do all four, you're ready.
m2-l1:
How does Scratch know where "over there" is? You can't tell a computer "move a bit to the left, near the tree." You need an exact address, like a spot on a treasure map. This week you'll learn Scratch's map, then use it to move sprites anywhere and change how they look.

Sprites and the stage

A sprite is anything that can move or do things: a character, a ball, a button, a cloud. Each sprite has its own scripts, costumes, and sounds.

The stage is the background where sprites live. The stage can have scripts too, but it can't move. It changes by switching backdrops.

You can add sprites three ways with the cat-face button at the bottom of the sprite pane:

  • Choose a Sprite opens the library, full of ready-made sprites.
  • Paint opens the paint editor so you can draw your own.
  • Surprise picks a random sprite.

The stage is a map

The stage is 480 steps wide and 360 steps tall. Every spot has two numbers:

  • x says how far left or right. The left edge is -240, the middle is 0, the right edge is 240.
  • y says how far up or down. The bottom is -180, the middle is 0, the top is 180.

A quick way to remember: x goes across (like the letter x lies flat), y goes up to the sky. Negative numbers mean left or down.

Tip

Move your mouse over the stage while you're in the Sensing category. The mouse x and mouse y blocks let you check the numbers. Easier still: drag a sprite and watch its x and y change in the sprite pane.

Motion blocks

Motion blocks (blue) move and turn sprites. Here are the ones you'll use most:

Block What it does
move (10) steps Walks forward in the direction the sprite faces
turn right (15) degrees Spins clockwise
go to x: (0) y: (0) Jumps instantly to a spot
glide (1) secs to x: (0) y: (0) Slides smoothly to a spot
change x by (10) Moves right (or left, with a negative number)
change y by (10) Moves up (or down, with a negative number)
set x to (0) Jumps left/right but keeps the same y
point in direction (90) Faces a direction: 90 right, -90 left, 0 up, 180 down

"Go to" versus "glide"

go to is like teleporting: no time passes. glide is like walking: you see the trip. Use go to to set a starting spot, and glide when you want the movement to be part of the show.

Why start with a "go to"?

Scratch remembers where a sprite was when the last run ended. If your script only moves the cat right, it will march a bit further right every time you click the flag, until it's stuck at the edge. Starting with go to x: () y: () puts it back at the starting line every time.

Costumes

A costume is one picture of a sprite. The cat has two: costume1 and costume2. Its legs are in different spots in each one. Flip between them quickly and the cat looks like it's walking.

Open the Costumes tab to see them. You can draw on them, change colors, or add new ones.

What happens:

The wait (0.3) seconds block comes from Control. Without it, the costume changes happen too fast to see. Next week, loops will let us repeat this without stacking the same blocks again and again.

Backdrops

A backdrop is a costume for the stage. Add one with the Choose a Backdrop button at the bottom right. A sprite can switch the backdrop too, which is great for stories that change scenes.

If your project has a second backdrop, the scene changes after the cat speaks. If there's only one, nothing seems to happen, so add a second one first.

Looks blocks

Looks blocks (purple) change how a sprite appears:

  • say [Hi!] for (2) seconds and think [Hmm...] for (2) seconds show bubbles.
  • change size by (10) and set size to (100) % make sprites grow or shrink.
  • change [color v] effect by (25) tints the sprite. Other effects in the dropdown include ghost (see-through), fisheye, whirl, and pixelate.
  • clear graphic effects puts everything back to normal.
  • show and hide make sprites appear and disappear.
  • go to [front v] layer puts a sprite in front of all the others.

What happens:

The first two blocks reset the cat so it doesn't keep growing every time you click the flag.

What usually goes wrong

  • Mixing up x and y. If your sprite goes up when you wanted right, you changed y instead of x.
  • Forgetting the minus sign. change x by (-10) moves left. change x by (10) moves right.
  • Effects that pile up. Size and color effects stay after the project stops. Reset them at the start of your script.
  • Editing the wrong sprite. The Costumes tab shows costumes for the selected sprite only. Check which sprite is highlighted.

Further reading

  • Coordinate System on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): more about x and y, with pictures.
  • Motion Blocks on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): every Motion block explained.
  • Looks Blocks on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): every Looks block, including all the graphic effects.
m2-l2:
Our cat has a dream: it wants to go to space. Today you'll make that happen with a short animated story in two scenes. You'll use everything from this week's Notes: x and y, gliding, costumes, backdrops, and Looks effects.

Here's the plan:

  1. Scene 1, the park. The cat walks in, talks, and blasts off out the top of the stage.
  2. Scene 2, space. The backdrop changes to stars, and the cat floats in, small and see-through, like it's far away.

Step 1: Set the scenes

Start a new project (File > New).

  1. Click Choose a Backdrop (bottom right).
  2. Search for Blue Sky and click it.
  3. Click Choose a Backdrop again and pick Stars.

Now your stage has three backdrops: the plain white backdrop1, Blue Sky, and Stars. Click the cat in the sprite pane so you're writing code for the cat, not the stage.

Tip

If you can't find those exact backdrops, pick any outdoor one and any space one. Just choose your backdrop names in the dropdowns below instead of ours.

Step 2: The reset script

Every good story starts the same way every time. These blocks put the cat back in its starting spot, at normal size, with no leftover effects:

Click the green flag. The stage shows the blue sky, and the cat sits near the bottom-left corner. Try dragging the cat somewhere else, then click the flag again. It jumps right back. That's the point of a reset script.

Step 3: Walk into the scene

Now we make the cat walk, switching costumes so its legs move. Keep adding to the bottom of the same script:

Click the flag. The cat takes four steps to the right, legs flipping each time, and ends up at x = -80.

How do we know it's -80? It started at -200 and moved 30 four times: -200 + 120 = -80. Check the x box in the sprite pane to see it yourself.

Notice we did the same three blocks four times. That's a lot of dragging! Next week, the repeat block will do this for us.

Step 4: The cat talks

Add speech and thought bubbles:

Click the flag and watch the whole thing so far:

Step 5: Blast off

The cat zooms straight up and disappears. We use glide for the zoom and hide so it vanishes at the top:

The x stays at -80 so the cat flies straight up, not sideways. A short glide time (half a second) makes it feel fast.

Watch out

Scratch won't let a sprite glide all the way off the stage. It always keeps a little bit showing at the edge. That's why we hide the cat once it reaches the top.

Step 6: Scene 2, in space

Change the backdrop, move the cat to the bottom while it's hidden, then bring it back looking far away:

Now the cat appears at the bottom, half its normal size and a little see-through, and drifts up into the middle of space.

Step 7: The ending

Finish with a spin and a final line:

Four quarter-turns make one full spin. The color change makes the cat glow a new color, like space changed it.

The whole script

Here is everything together, top to bottom. Yours should match this (with your own words if you changed them):

Test it like a director

Click the green flag twice in a row. Does the story look the same both times? If the second run starts in space or with a tiny cat, a reset block is missing at the top. Compare your blocks to the list above.

Common bugs

  • The cat starts in space on the second run. You're missing switch backdrop to (Blue Sky v) at the top.
  • The cat is invisible. You're missing show in the reset, so it stayed hidden from the last run.
  • The cat flies off at an angle. The x in your blast-off glide doesn't match where the cat is standing. It should be -80.
  • The cat is upside down at the end. You have three or five turn blocks instead of four.

Make it yours

  • Change what the cat says.
  • Use a different sprite as the space traveler.
  • Add a third scene with another backdrop, like the cat landing on a planet.

Save your project as week1-space-cat.sb3 (or File > Save now with an account).

  • Backdrop on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): adding and switching stage backgrounds.
  • Glide () Secs to X: () Y: () on the Scratch Wiki (opens in a new tab): all about the glide block.

m3-l1:
A video game doesn't do anything until you press a button. Then it reacts: you press the right arrow, the hero runs. You press space, the hero jumps. Those button presses are called events, and this week your projects start listening for them. You'll also learn loops, which let one small script run over and over, and sounds that play at just the right moment.

Events: when should a script start?

Events are the yellow hat blocks in the Events category. A hat block sits on top of a script and waits. When its event happens, the script below it runs.

Hat block Runs when...
when green flag clicked someone clicks the green flag
when [space v] key pressed someone presses that key
when this sprite clicked someone clicks on this sprite
when backdrop switches to [backdrop1 v] the stage changes to that backdrop
when stage clicked someone clicks the stage (this one is only for the Stage)

A sprite can have many scripts, each with its own hat. They all wait at the same time. That's how one sprite can walk with the arrow keys and meow when clicked.

What happens:

That's four separate scripts in one sprite. Spread them out in the code area so they don't touch.

Watch out

When the cat faces left (point in direction (-90)), it turns upside down! Fix it by adding set rotation style [left-right v] from Motion to your green flag script. Now the cat flips to face left instead of rolling over.

Loops: do it again (and again)

Remember stacking move, next costume, wait four times last week? Loops fix that. They're the C-shaped blocks in Control. Blocks you put inside the "mouth" of the C get repeated.

repeat

repeat (10) runs the blocks inside it exactly that many times, then moves on to the next block.

What happens:

forever

forever repeats the blocks inside it until you click the red stop sign. There's no bottom bump, so nothing can go after it.

The cat walks in place forever, like it's on a treadmill.

Animation = costume + wait + loop

This pattern is the heart of animation in Scratch:

  1. next costume changes the picture.
  2. wait slows it down so your eyes can see it. Smaller numbers mean faster animation.
  3. A loop keeps it going.

Many library sprites (like the Bat, Parrot, or Butterfly) have several costumes made for this. Open their Costumes tab and look.

Bounce off the walls

Put if on edge, bounce inside a forever loop and a sprite will zoom around the stage, turning around whenever it hits an edge:

The cat moves at an angle, bouncing off all four edges like a screensaver, until you click stop.

Sounds and timing

Sound blocks are pink. Each sprite starts with its own sounds. Add more from the Sounds tab with the Choose a Sound button at the bottom.

There are two ways to play a sound, and the difference matters:

  • start sound (Meow v) begins the sound and immediately goes on to the next block.
  • play sound (Meow v) until done waits until the sound is finished before going on.

Compare these two scripts:

What happens:

Use start sound when you want the sound and the action to happen together. Use play sound until done when you want things to happen in order, like notes in a song.

What usually goes wrong

m4-l1:
Every morning you make decisions: if it's raining, take an umbrella, else wear sunglasses. Games make decisions like that thousands of times a minute. If the player touches the coin, collect it. If the ball hits the wall, bounce. This week your sprites learn to look around, ask questions, and choose what to do.

Yes-or-no questions

Some blocks are shaped like a stretched hexagon with pointy ends. These are boolean blocks, also called conditions. They don't do anything. They answer a yes-or-no question with true or false.

Here are some from Sensing:

  • <touching (mouse-pointer v)?> is the sprite touching the mouse, another sprite, or the edge?
  • <touching color [#ff0000]?> is the sprite touching that color?
  • <key (space v) pressed?> is that key being held down right now?
  • <mouse down?> is the mouse button pressed?

And some from Operators that compare numbers:

  • <(x position) > (200)> is x bigger than 200?
  • <(x position) < (-200)> is x smaller than -200?
  • <(answer) = [yes]> is the answer exactly "yes"?

Click any boolean block in the palette and Scratch shows you whether it's true or false right now. Try it with touching (mouse-pointer v)? while your mouse is over the cat.

if/then: do it only sometimes

The if <> then block in Control has a hexagon-shaped hole. Drop a condition in it. The blocks inside only run when the condition is true.

What happens:

That's not quite right. We need a way to say something else when the mouse is away.

if/else: pick one of two

if <> then with an else part has two mouths. Exactly one of them runs each time: the top one if the condition is true, the bottom one if it's false.

What happens:

An empty say [] block removes the speech bubble.

Why forever + if?

An if only checks once, at the moment it runs. Put it inside a forever loop and it checks over and over, many times a second. This "forever-if" pattern is how almost every game watches for things to happen.

Smooth movement with key pressed?

Last week, when [right arrow v] key pressed moved the cat. It works, but there's a pause before the key starts repeating, and you can only press one key at a time. Games use a forever loop with key pressed? instead:

Now the cat glides smoothly while you hold a key, and holding up and right together moves it diagonally.

Asking questions

ask [What's your name?] and wait shows a question with a text box. Whatever the player types is saved in the answer block, which you can use like any value.

What happens if you type yes:

What happens if you type no (or anything else):

The = block doesn't care about capital letters, so YES and Yes count too.

Collisions: when things touch

A collision is when two things on the stage overlap. Scratch has three main ways to check.

Touching another sprite

Pick the sprite's name in the touching dropdown. Here the cat is chasing a sprite called Apple:

The cat follows your mouse. Lead it to the apple, and the cat says "Yum!" and jumps somewhere random.

Touching a color

touching color is perfect for walls, lava, and finish lines that are part of the backdrop. To pick the color, click the color circle in the block, then click the eyedropper at the bottom and click that color on the stage.

If the sprite touches red, it goes back to the start. This block needs to be inside a forever loop to keep checking.

Touching the edge

<touching (edge v)?> is true when any part of the sprite reaches the side of the stage. You can also check the position yourself. This stops the cat at an invisible wall:

The cat moves right but never past x = 200, as if it bumped into glass.

Tip

if on edge, bounce is an easy shortcut for bouncing, but it only works for the stage edges. To bounce off a paddle or wall sprite, use something like if <touching (Paddle v)?> then and turn the sprite yourself.

What usually goes wrong

  • The if only works once. You forgot the forever loop around it.
  • touching color never turns true. The color isn't an exact match. Use the eyedropper instead of guessing.
  • The sprite gets "stuck" on a wall. After a collision, move it back out (for example, change x by (-5)) so it's not still touching next time around.
  • Both if/else parts seem to run. You probably used two separate if blocks. In if/else, only one part can ever run.
  • The sprite you want isn't in the touching dropdown. A sprite can't check if it's touching itself, so its own name never shows up there. Make sure you're editing the right sprite.

Today you'll draw your own maze, then write the code that makes it work: walls you can't walk through, edges that send you back to start, and a goal that says "Almost there!" as you get close. By the end, someone else can play it.

Step 1: Draw the maze

The walls are part of the backdrop, so we draw them on the Stage.

  1. Start a new project (File > New).
  2. Click the Stage button in the bottom right, then open the Backdrops tab.
  3. Pick the Rectangle tool. Set the Fill to one bright color, like blue. Use this color for every wall.
  4. Draw thick wall rectangles to make a path from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner. Leave the path wide, at least as wide as two fingers on the screen.

Tip

Make your first maze easy, with only three or four turns. You can always make a harder one later. A maze that's too hard to test is a maze you can't finish building!

Step 2: Set up the player and goal

  2. Add the Ball sprite from the library. In the sprite pane, rename it Player and set its size to 40.
  3. Drag the player to the start of your maze, at the top left. Write down the x and y numbers shown in the sprite pane. We'll use x: -200, y: 140.
  4. Add the Star sprite (or any sprite you like) and rename it Goal. Drag it to the end of your maze, at the bottom right. We'll use x: 200, y: -140.

Put a touching color check inside each arrow's if. For the color, click the color circle in the block, click the eyedropper at the bottom of the color menu, then click one of your walls on the stage.

m5-l1:
Every game you love keeps track of something. Mario counts coins. Minecraft counts hearts. A race game counts down the seconds. Your Scratch projects can do the same thing, and this week you learn how. You'll also learn how one sprite can "shout" a message to all the others, so they can work as a team.

What is a variable?

A variable is a box with a name on it. Inside the box is one value, like 0 or 3 or 25. Your scripts can look inside the box, put a new value in, or add to it.

In Scratch, variables live in the orange Variables category. To make one:

  1. Click Variables in the block list.
  2. Click Make a Variable.
  3. Type a name, like score.
  4. Pick For all sprites (you'll see why below).
  5. Click OK.

A new score block appears. There's also a checkbox next to it. When the box is checked, a little display called a monitor shows the variable on the stage, so players can see it.

Tip

Right-click the monitor on the stage and choose large readout to show just the number. It looks more like a real game.

The four variable blocks you need

  • set throws away the old value and puts in a new one.
  • change adds to the value. Use a negative number, like -1, to subtract.
  • show variable and hide variable turn the monitor on and off from a script.

The round (score) reporter block gives you the value inside the box. You can drop it into any round hole, like say or an if test.

Keeping score

Here's a tiny game. Click the cat to earn points.

Click the cat three times and the monitor shows:

Notice the first script. It resets the score every time you click the green flag. Without it, the score keeps going from the last game, so your second game starts at 3 instead of 0.

Watch out

The number one variable bug: forgetting to reset. Every variable your game uses should get a set block right under when green flag clicked.

Lives: counting down

Lives work like score, but backward. You start with a few and lose one each time something bad happens. Then you check if you've run out.

Why go to x: (0) y: (0) after losing a life? If the sprite stays on the shark, the loop runs again a split second later, sees it's still touching, and takes another life. Moving away stops that. This is a very common surprise.

Timers: two ways

Your own countdown variable

Make a variable called time left. Then:

The monitor counts 30, 29, 28... all the way to 0. Then the sprite says "Time's up!". This kind of timer is easy for players to read.

Scratch's built-in timer

Scratch also has a stopwatch that's always running. It's in the light-blue Sensing category.

reset timer sets the stopwatch back to 0. The (timer) block reports seconds with decimals, like 4.37. It's great for "how fast did you finish?" games.

Broadcast: sprites sending messages

So far, each sprite only knows about itself. But games need teamwork. When the game ends, the player should stop, the enemies should disappear, and the stage should show a "Game Over" screen. How does everyone find out?

With broadcast. One sprite sends a message, and every sprite (and the stage) can listen for it. These blocks are in the yellow Events category.

To make a new message, click the little arrow on broadcast, choose New message, and type a name like game over.

Here's how it works in a game. The player sprite notices the lives ran out and tells everyone:

Then each sprite decides what to do with the news. The stage changes the picture:

And the enemy sprite hides:

The player didn't need to know anything about the stage or the enemy. It just sent the message. That keeps your scripts short and easy to fix.

Broadcast and wait

There's a second version: broadcast (get ready v) and wait. It sends the message, then pauses until every script that received it has finished. Use it when order matters, like showing a "3, 2, 1, go!" countdown before the game starts.

"For all sprites" vs. "For this sprite only"

When you make a variable, Scratch asks this question.

  • For all sprites means every sprite can see and change it. Use this for score, lives, and time left, because lots of sprites need them.
  • For this sprite only means only that one sprite owns it. Use it for something private, like how fast one enemy moves.

If your score never changes when a coin is touched, check this first. The coin may be changing its own private copy.

Quick recap

  • Variables hold numbers your game needs to remember.
  • Always set them when the green flag is clicked.
  • change adds or subtracts.
  • broadcast sends a message. when I receive listens for it.

Apples are falling from the sky, and you have one bowl. Catch an apple and you score a point. Miss one and you lose a life. You have 30 seconds. When time runs out or your lives hit zero, a big GAME OVER screen appears.

That's the game we're building today. It uses everything from this week's notes: three variables and one broadcast message.

Step 1: Set up the project

  1. Open a new project in Scratch.
  2. Delete the cat. Right-click it in the sprite list and choose delete.
  3. Click Choose a Sprite and add Bowl. Then add Apple.
  4. Click Choose a Backdrop (bottom right) and add Blue Sky.
  5. Now make a second backdrop. Hover over the backdrop button and pick the paintbrush (Paint). Use the Text tool to write GAME OVER in big letters. At the top of the paint editor, rename this backdrop to Game Over.

You should now have two sprites (Bowl, Apple) and backdrops named Blue Sky and Game Over.

Tip

Name things carefully. Your scripts pick backdrops by name, so Game Over and game over are different to you, and a messy list makes bugs harder to find.

Step 2: Make the variables

Click Variables, then Make a Variable three times. Make each one For all sprites:

  • score
  • lives
  • time left

Keep all three checkboxes ticked so their monitors show on the stage. Drag the monitors to the top-left corner so they don't cover the apples.

Step 3: Move the bowl

Click the Bowl sprite and build this script:

Click the green flag. The bowl jumps to the bottom middle of the stage. Hold the arrow keys and it slides left and right.

Why two separate if blocks instead of one if/else? With two, the game checks both keys every time around the loop. It feels smoother.

Step 4: The stage runs the clock

The stage is a great place for "whole game" jobs, like resetting variables and running the timer. Click the Stage (on the right, under the stage preview) and build this:

To make the game over message, click the arrow on the broadcast block, choose New message, and type game over.

Click the green flag and watch the monitors:

Watch out

Don't skip switch backdrop to (Blue Sky v). After your first game ends, the stage is stuck on the Game Over backdrop. This block puts the sky back when you play again.

Step 5: Make the apple fall

Click the Apple sprite. This is the biggest script in the game, so build it slowly.

Here's what each part does:

  1. show makes sure the apple is visible. (It hides at game over, so it must come back.)
  2. go to x: (pick random...) y: (180) puts the apple at the top in a random spot.

Picture a snowstorm with 50 snowflakes. You could add 50 snowflake sprites and copy the same script into each one. But then, if you want them to fall a little faster, you'd have to fix 50 scripts! There's a much better way. This week you'll learn two power tools: clones, which make copies of a sprite while the game runs, and My Blocks, which let you invent your own blocks.

Part 1: Clones

A clone is a copy of a sprite that Scratch makes while your project is running. The clone looks like the sprite and runs the sprite's clone scripts. When the clone's job is done, it disappears. You only build the scripts once.

Three orange Control blocks do all the work:

  • create clone of (myself v) makes a new copy. You can also pick another sprite's name from the dropdown to clone that sprite instead.
  • when I start as a clone is a hat block. Only clones run the scripts under it. The original sprite never does.
  • delete this clone removes the clone. Each clone should delete itself when it's finished.

A snowstorm in two scripts

Paint a small white circle and name the sprite Snowflake. Pick a dark backdrop so you can see it.

Click the green flag. Thirty snowflakes drift down, one every 0.2 seconds, each starting in a different spot.

Let's look at what happened:

  1. The original Snowflake hides. Think of it as a hidden factory that makes the clones.
  2. The repeat (30) loop makes 30 clones.
  3. Each clone runs when I start as a clone on its own. It picks its own spot, shows itself, falls, and deletes itself at the bottom.

Watch out

A clone starts as an exact copy of its parent, including being hidden. If you forget show in the clone script, your clones exist but you can't see them. If nothing appears on screen, check this first.

Clones copy everything

When a clone is born, it copies the parent's position, direction, costume, size, effects, and whether it's showing. That's why the snowflake clones start wherever the original was, and why we move them right away.

Clones also get their own copy of any variable made For this sprite only. That means every clone can have its own value. Make a speed variable, choose For this sprite only, and try this:

Now some flakes fall slowly and some zoom. Each clone remembers its own speed. A For all sprites variable is different: there's only one, and every clone shares it. That's what you want for score.

Clones hear messages too

Clones run every hat block in the sprite except when green flag clicked. That includes when I receive, when this sprite clicked, and when [space v] key pressed. This is handy: one when I receive [game over v] with delete this clone clears every clone at once.

But it can also surprise you:

The first time you press space, you get one clone. But now there are two copies of the sprite listening for space. Press again, and both make a clone, so you have four. Then eight. Then sixteen! To avoid this, put the when [space v] key pressed script in a sprite that never gets cloned, and use create clone of (Laser v) from there. You'll do exactly that in the code-along.

The 300 clone limit

Scratch allows up to 300 clones at once. After that, create clone of quietly does nothing. If your clones never delete themselves, you'll hit the limit and new clones will stop appearing. Always give every clone a way to end with delete this clone.

The good news: clicking the green flag or the red stop sign wipes out all clones, so each game starts clean.

Part 2: My Blocks

Sometimes you need the same group of blocks in many places. My Blocks (the pink category at the bottom) let you bundle them up under a new name.

Making a block

  1. Click My Blocks, then Make a Block.
  2. Type a name, like jump.
  3. Click Add an input number or text and name it height.
  4. Click OK.

A pink define hat appears in your code area. Whatever you snap under it is what your new block does.

Now use it like any other block:

Press space for a small hop. Press the up arrow for a big leap. Both use the same define script, just with a different height.

Why bother?

  • Shorter scripts. jump (60) is easier to read than 8 blocks of math.
  • Fix it once. If the jump looks too fast, change the define script and every jump is fixed.
  • Good names explain your code. A script that says reset player tells you what it does without reading every block.

A My Block with no inputs

Inputs are optional. This block puts a player back at the start:

You can call reset player when the green flag is clicked, when the player loses a life, and when a new level starts.

Things to know

  • My Blocks belong to one sprite. A block made in the Cat doesn't show up in the Dog. To share it, drag the define script onto the Dog in the sprite list. Scratch copies it over.
  • Inputs only work inside their define script. The (height) reporter means nothing anywhere else. Drag it from the define hat, not from Variables.
  • To change a block, right-click the define hat and choose Edit.
  • Run without screen refresh is a checkbox in the Make a Block window. It makes the block finish instantly without showing each step. Leave it off for movement like jump, or you won't see the jump happen.

Clones and My Blocks together

These two tools work great as a team. Here's a block that makes a whole group of clones:

Use Add a label in the Make a Block window to put the word "flakes" after the input. Now spawn (10) flakes reads almost like a sentence.

What turns a fun demo into a real game? Three things. The player needs a goal to reach, a way to lose, and a challenge that grows. Then the game needs testing by someone who isn't you. And finally, you get to share it. This week covers all of that.

Levels

A level is a stage of the game with its own layout or difficulty. Most Scratch games track the level with one variable, level, and one message that sets everything up.

Each sprite listens for start level and gets ready for whichever level it is. The stage picks the right backdrop:

To move up a level, change the variable and send the message again:

This pattern is powerful because adding Level 3 later means adding one more if in each sprite. Nothing else changes.

Making later levels harder

You don't always need new backdrops. You can use the level number in your math, so the game speeds up by itself:

Level 1 falls 2 steps at a time. Level 2 falls 4. Level 3 falls 6. One block, endless levels.

Other easy ways to raise the difficulty:

  • Shorter time on the clock.
  • More clones per wave.
  • Smaller targets with set size to.
  • A new obstacle that only shows up when level is greater than 1.

Winning and losing

Every game needs clear endings. Players should never wonder, "Wait, did I win?"

A good ending has three parts:

  1. A check. Something like if <(lives) = (0)> or if <(level) > (2)>.
  2. A message. broadcast (game over v) or broadcast (you win v).
  3. A screen. A backdrop, a sound, or a sprite that says what happened.

You can also start scripts from the backdrop itself with this hat:

Tip

Test your endings first, not last. Temporarily set [lives v] to (1) so you can lose fast, or start at the final level so you can win fast. Just remember to change it back.

Playtesting

Playtesting means watching someone else play your game. It's the fastest way to find out what's confusing. You know how your game works, so you can't see it the way a new player does.

How to run a good playtest:

  1. Give the player your instructions, then stay quiet. Don't explain. If they're confused, that's useful information.
  2. Watch their face and hands. Where do they get stuck? Where do they smile?
  3. Write down what happens, not what you wish happened.
  4. Afterward, ask: "What was the most fun part? What was confusing? Was it too easy or too hard?"

Simple playtest notes look like this:

Debugging

A bug is when your game doesn't do what you meant. Every coder writes bugs, even experts. The skill is finding them.

Detective tricks

  • Make it happen again. Find the exact steps that cause the bug. "When I touch the wall on level 2, the score resets."

  • Watch your variables. Check the box next to a variable so its monitor shows on the stage. Watch it change as you play.

  • Make sprites talk. Drop a say block in to show what a sprite "thinks":

  • Click one script. Clicking a script runs just that script, and it glows yellow while it runs. If it never stops glowing, it's stuck in a loop.

  • Slow it down. Add a wait (0.5) seconds inside a loop to watch each step. Take it out when you're done.

The usual suspects

Most Scratch bugs are one of these:

Bug Likely cause
Works the first time, broken the second A variable or backdrop isn't reset under the green flag
A sprite is missing It was hidden last game and never told to show
A message does nothing Sender and receiver picked different message names
Score changes in one sprite but not another The variable was made "For this sprite only"
Lives drop to 0 in one hit Still touching the enemy, so the loop counts it again and again
Clones stop appearing They never delete this clone, so you hit the 300 limit

Fix one thing at a time, then test again. If you change five things and it works, you won't know which one was the fix.

Sharing and remixing responsibly

When your game is ready, you can share it on the Scratch website so anyone can play. You need a Scratch account for this, so ask a parent or guardian first.

Before you click Share

On your project page, fill in:

  • Instructions: which keys to press and what the goal is.
  • Notes and Credits: who made what. If you used someone else's art, music, or code, name them here.

The Scratch community guidelines

Scratch is a community of millions of kids. Its guidelines boil down to a few big ideas:

  • Be respectful. Treat everyone kindly, in projects and in comments.
  • Keep personal information private. Never share your real full name, address, phone number, school, passwords, or photos of yourself. Your username is enough.
  • Give helpful feedback. Say what you liked, and suggest ideas kindly.
  • Embrace remixing and give credit. Building on others' work is welcome, and credit is how you say thank you.
  • Be honest. Don't pretend someone else's project is yours.
  • Help keep Scratch friendly. Use the Report button if you see something mean or unsafe. Don't argue back.

Remixing the right way

The Remix button on any shared project makes your own copy to change. Scratch automatically adds a link back to the original. To be a great remixer:

  • Change something real: new levels, new art, a new rule.
  • Say what you changed and thank the original creator in Notes and Credits.
  • Never remove someone's credit from a project you remixed.

Not sharing online?

That's totally fine. Use File > Save to your computer to download your game as a .sb3 file. You can open it later with File > Load from your computer, or send the file to your teacher.

For six weeks you've built other people's game ideas: a catching game, a space shooter, a maze. Now it's your turn to be the game designer. You get to decide what the player is, what they're trying to do, and what's standing in their way.

This lesson is all about planning. Real game studios spend days planning before they build anything. A good plan means fewer "uh-oh" moments later.

The brief

Make an original game in Scratch 3. It can be about anything you like, as long as it's kind and safe for everyone. Your game must include all of these:

Requirement What it means Where you learned it
Instructions The player knows how to play: on a title screen, in a speech bubble, or on the project page Week 6
Score or timer A variable the player can see that counts points or time Week 4
Collisions Something happens when sprites touch each other, a color, or the edge Weeks 1–3
A clone At least one sprite makes copies of itself or another sprite Week 5
A My Block At least one block you defined yourself and actually use Week 5
Two levels At least two levels that look or play differently Week 6
Win and lose A clear winning ending and a clear losing ending Week 6

What you turn in

  1. Your game: a shared Scratch link, or your .sb3 file from File > Save to your computer.
  2. Playtest notes: what happened when at least one other person played your game.
  3. One fix: a short note about one thing you changed because of playtesting.

Pick an idea

Here are some ideas that fit the brief. Borrow one, mix two, or invent your own.

  • Bug Catcher. Bugs crawl across a garden (clones). Click them for points before the timer runs out. Level 2 adds fast bugs and a bee you must not click.
  • Meteor Dodge. Meteors fall (clones), and you steer a spaceship to dodge them. Survive 30 seconds to reach Level 2, where meteors come from both sides.
  • Deep Sea Diver. Swim around collecting pearls. Sharks patrol. Level 2 is deeper and darker, with more sharks.
  • Pizza Rush. Toppings fall from the sky. Catch the right ones, avoid the burnt ones. Make 3 pizzas to win.
  • Ghost House. A maze with ghosts that glide back and forth. Find the key to open the door to Level 2.
  • Snowball Fight. Throw snowball clones at targets that pop up. Hit 10 to move on.

Tip

Choose the smaller idea. A simple game that works and feels polished beats a giant game that's half finished. You can always add more once the basics work.

Step 1: Write your pitch

A pitch is one or two sentences that explain your game. If you can't say it simply, the idea might be too big.

Step 2: Match your idea to the requirements

Go down the brief's list and write how your game will meet each one. Here's the plan for Bug Catcher:

If a row is empty, change your idea until every row is filled.

Step 3: Draw a storyboard

A storyboard is a set of quick sketches, like a comic strip, showing each screen of your game. Grab paper and fold it into six boxes. Draw one screen in each:

Stick figures and boxes are perfect. Nobody's grading your drawing. Draw arrows to show which way things move, and label the sprites.

Step 4: List your sprites, backdrops, and variables

Before you open Scratch, write down what you'll need. This becomes your checklist while building.

Step 5: Plan your first script

Most games start the same way: show a title screen, wait for the player, then start Level 1. You can build this today. Put it on the Stage:

Paint a backdrop called Title with your game's name and "Press SPACE to start." Click the green flag. The title shows and nothing happens until you press space. Then the start level message goes out, ready for your sprites to listen to.

This one script already covers two requirements: instructions and resetting your variables.

Check your plan with a buddy

Before you build, show your pitch and storyboard to a classmate, a sibling, or your instructor. Ask:

  • Does my game sound fun?
  • Is anything confusing?
  • Is it small enough to finish?

Change your plan if you need to. Changing a drawing takes 30 seconds. Changing a finished game takes much longer.

Big games are built the same way you'd build a LEGO castle: one section at a time, checking each part is solid before adding the next. In coding, those sections are called milestones. After each one, your game should run without errors, even if it isn't finished.

Below, each milestone is shown with an example game called Meteor Dodge: steer a ship, dodge falling meteors, survive 20 seconds on each of two levels. Your game will be different, but the pattern for each milestone is the same. Use these scripts as a starting point and change them to fit your idea.

Tip

After each milestone, use File > Save to your computer and add the milestone number to the file name, like meteor-dodge-m2.sb3. If you break something later, you can go back.

  • Backdrops: a painted Title (game name plus how to play), Level 1, Level 2, You Win, and Game Over. For Meteor Dodge, add Stars and one more space backdrop from the library and rename them Level 1 and Level 2.

Your game runs. Congratulations! But "it runs on my computer when I play it" is not the same as "it's fun for someone who's never seen it." The last stretch of any game project is testing, fixing, and showing it off. Game studios call this polish, and it's often what players remember most.

Round 1: Test it yourself

Before anyone else plays, try to break your own game. Go through this list and fix anything that fails.

  • Both endings. Win once. Lose once. Does each show the right screen and stop the game?
  • Play again. Click the green flag after each ending. Is every variable back to its starting value? Is every sprite visible and in the right place? Is the title or Level 1 backdrop showing?
  • Both levels. Does Level 2 actually look or play differently?
  • Weird players. Mash every key. Hold an arrow key the whole time. Don't touch anything at all. Does the game still behave?
  • Clones. Play for a few minutes. Do clones keep appearing, or do they stop (a sign they never get deleted)?

Tip

Testing a long game takes forever. Temporarily set time left to 5, or start on level 2, so you can reach the endings fast. Write yourself a note to change these back.

Round 2: A real playtest

Find at least one person who hasn't played your game: a family member, a friend, or a classmate in breakout rooms. Two testers is even better.

Follow the playtest rules from Week 6:

  1. Let them read your instructions. Don't explain anything else.
  2. Watch quietly. Your job is to notice, not to help.
  3. Write down what they do and say.
  4. At the end, ask three questions: What was fun? What was confusing? Too easy, too hard, or just right?

Use this template for your playtest notes. These notes are part of what you turn in.

Pick your one fix

Your tester probably found several things. You need to make at least one fix, and write it up. Pick the one that matters most, in this order:

  1. Broken: something doesn't work, like a sprite missing on the second game.
  2. Unfair or confusing: the player didn't know what to do, or lost for no good reason.
  3. Too easy or too hard: speeds, timers, or numbers of clones.
  4. Looks and sounds: nice to have, but last.

Example fix

In the notes above, the tester got hit right as Level 2 began. Meteors appear before the player is ready. The fix: give the player a one-second head start before spawning begins.

Polish checklist

With time left over, pick a few:

  • Sounds for scoring, getting hit, winning, and losing.
  • A "Level 2!" message so players notice the change.
  • A "Click the green flag to play again" line on your ending backdrops.
  • Tidy code: right-click the code area and choose Clean up Blocks. Delete leftover test scripts.
  • Make sure the monitors don't cover anything important.

Save it or share it

To turn in a file: use File > Save to your computer. You'll get a .sb3 file. Give it a clear name, like meteor-dodge-final.sb3.

To share a link (only with a Scratch account and a grown-up's okay):

  1. Click Share in the editor.
  2. On the project page, fill in Instructions and Notes and Credits.
  3. In Notes and Credits, name anything you didn't make yourself: library sprites are fine to use, but if you remixed someone's project or used their art or music, thank them by username.
  4. Check that nothing on the page, in sprites, or in your backdrops shows your real name, school, location, or photos of you.
  5. Copy the link from your browser's address bar.

Presenting your game

You'll have about two minutes to show your game to the class. Use this plan:

  1. Pitch (15 seconds): your one-sentence description.
  2. Demo (60 seconds): play a bit of Level 1 and show Level 2. Show one ending.
  3. Code tour (20 seconds): show one script you're proud of, like your My Block or clone script.
  4. Playtest fix (15 seconds): what your tester found and how you fixed it.
  5. Next time (10 seconds): one thing you'd add if you had another week.

Watch out

Demos love to break when people are watching. Practice once beforehand, and keep a copy of your last working .sb3 file ready to load with File > Load from your computer, just in case.

Grading checklist

Check every box before you turn in your project.

The game

  • Instructions tell the player the keys, the goal, and how to win.
  • A score or timer variable is visible on screen and works.
  • At least one collision does something (touching a sprite, a color, or the edge).
  • At least one sprite uses clones, and the clones get deleted.
  • At least one My Block is defined and used.
  • At least two levels that look or play differently.
  • A clear win ending and a clear lose ending.
  • Clicking the green flag again starts a fresh game.

What you turn in

  • A shared Scratch link or a .sb3 file.
  • Playtest notes from at least one tester.
  • A write-up of one fix: the problem, what you changed, and whether it worked.

Being a good Scratcher

  • Credit given for anything you didn't make yourself.
  • No personal information anywhere in the project or its page.
